articles.title: Rafale F4.2 for 114 Jets: Is India Investing Too Much in 4.5-Generation Fighters?
articles.text:
India’s fighter-modernisation strategy is approaching an important contradiction. On one side, the Indian Air Force faces an immediate numerical crisis, with its fighter strength well below the authorised level. On the other, India’s future combat-aircraft strategy is increasingly centred on the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) and other next-generation systems designed to operate in an environment where conventional 4.5-generation fighters may face increasing survivability challenges.
That raises a legitimate question: if India believes the future battlefield is moving rapidly toward fifth-generation combat aviation, is procuring 114 additional Rafale fighters in an F4.2 configuration the best way to solve the IAF’s long-term numerical problem?
The question has become more relevant following France’s submission of its technical and commercial proposal for 114 Rafales under the MRFA requirement, with 94 aircraft reportedly intended for production in India.
The answer is not necessarily that Rafale is obsolete. It is not. Rafale F4 represents a highly capable 4.5-generation combat aircraft with sophisticated sensors, electronic warfare, networking and modern weapons. The issue is opportunity cost.
India could spend enormous resources acquiring another large fleet of fourth-generation-plus fighters while simultaneously attempting to accelerate its fifth-generation indigenous capability.
That deserves a strategic debate.
The AMCA Mk1 is expected to use the GE F414, with current plans centred on an initial batch of approximately 40 aircraft. A more powerful engine in the 110–120 kN class is intended for the later AMCA Mk2.
This creates an interesting possibility.
Instead of treating the first 40 AMCA Mk1 aircraft as a relatively small initial batch, India could attempt to accelerate the programme and dramatically expand the number of F414-powered AMCA Mk1 aircraft before transitioning to the higher-thrust AMCA Mk2.
Under such a strategy, the F414-powered AMCA would essentially become India’s bridge into fifth-generation combat aviation.
Even though the F414 is not a revolutionary fifth-generation engine, the aircraft around it is fundamentally different from Rafale. The AMCA’s value would come from its low-observable design, internal weapons carriage, sensor fusion, integrated electronic warfare and network-centric architecture rather than simply engine thrust.
This distinction is critical.
A fighter’s generation is not determined by its engine alone. A 98-kN-class engine does not automatically make an aircraft fourth generation. Similarly, installing a more powerful engine does not automatically make an aircraft fifth generation.
The combat system matters.
The F414 itself is a mature and extensively developed engine family. DRDO documentation notes that the F414 is based on the F404 architecture, has accumulated millions of flight hours across the family and provides substantially more thrust than the F404.
Therefore, the argument for increasing AMCA Mk1 production is not that the F414 is somehow equivalent to a future 110–120 kN fifth-generation engine. It is that India could use an already-selected, relatively mature engine to get a stealth fighter into production earlier, while simultaneously developing the more powerful indigenous/co-developed engine for later AMCA variants.
There is another important consideration: time.
The IAF cannot wait indefinitely for AMCA Mk2. India’s fighter squadron shortage exists today, whereas the higher-thrust AMCA variant remains a longer-term proposition. The first AMCA production aircraft themselves are still years away. Current reporting puts the initial AMCA Mk1 around the F414 and a later higher-thrust Mk2 around a new engine.
Consequently, the sensible alternative to Rafale is not simply “wait for AMCA.”
It would be accelerate AMCA Mk1 while continuing Rafale and Tejas Mk2 production at appropriate levels.
That could potentially give India three layers of combat aviation: Rafale and upgraded Su-30MKI providing immediate high-end 4.5-generation capability, Tejas Mk2 providing a larger indigenous 4.5-generation fleet, and AMCA progressively taking over the high-end survivability role.
The argument for buying Rafale remains strong from another perspective: India needs aircraft now.
A fighter squadron cannot be created by announcing a future programme. It requires aircraft, trained pilots, weapons, maintenance infrastructure and operational experience. Rafale is already a mature operational platform, and a large Indian production programme could potentially deliver aircraft substantially earlier than an accelerated AMCA programme.
This is the strongest case for the MRFA acquisition.
But there is an opportunity cost.
Every large capital allocation to Rafale potentially competes with funding for AMCA development, production infrastructure, weapons, unmanned combat aircraft, airborne early-warning platforms and electronic warfare capabilities.
And that is where India’s strategy needs to be more ambitious.
If India ultimately purchases 114 Rafales, it should not allow the programme to become a substitute for AMCA. The Rafale should instead be treated as a bridge capability whose numbers are deliberately limited by the time AMCA reaches mature production.
The alternative strategy would be to accelerate AMCA Mk1 dramatically and potentially expand the planned production run from roughly 40 aircraft to something closer to 100–120 F414-powered aircraft, subject to the aircraft’s test results and industrial capacity.
This would create a very different force structure.
Instead of waiting for AMCA Mk2 before producing the aircraft in substantial numbers, India could build an initial stealth-fighter fleet around the F414 and progressively upgrade the architecture, weapons and software while the higher-thrust engine matures.
There are significant risks. AMCA is considerably more complex than Rafale, and attempting to accelerate production before the aircraft has completed adequate testing could introduce unacceptable reliability and safety problems. India’s history with indigenous fighter programmes demonstrates why flight testing, certification and production qualification cannot simply be compressed indefinitely.
The engine issue is another major concern. Current reporting indicates that commercial negotiations over the F414 have faced cost complications, although other reporting has said claims of a complete negotiation deadlock are incorrect.
That means India should not assume that increasing AMCA Mk1 production automatically solves the problem. The F414 supply chain itself must first become reliable and scalable.
Nevertheless, the strategic question remains valid.
If India is going to spend heavily to close the fighter-number gap, it should ask whether some of that investment can simultaneously move the fleet toward fifth-generation capability rather than simply increase the size of the 4.5-generation fleet.
The ideal solution may therefore not be Rafale versus AMCA.
It could be fewer Rafales + more Tejas Mk2 + dramatically accelerated AMCA Mk1 + rapid transition to AMCA Mk2.
Rafale would provide immediate high-end combat power. Tejas Mk2 would supply numbers. AMCA Mk1 would introduce stealth and advanced sensor fusion at scale. AMCA Mk2 would eventually provide the higher-thrust fifth-generation capability India ultimately wants.
The danger lies in allowing the 114-Rafale programme to become the answer to every problem.
India’s fighter shortage is a numerical crisis, but it is also a generational-transition crisis. Solving only the number problem with another large 4.5-generation acquisition could leave India with a larger fleet but still facing the same technological transition a decade later.
The smarter objective should be to ensure that every year of additional fighter production also moves the IAF closer to a fifth-generation force.

articles.title: PAF’s Fighter Modernisation Problem: Why JF-17 Block III Numbers Are Still Limited
articles.text:
The Pakistan Air Force’s transition toward a more modern fighter fleet is facing a significant numerical challenge. While the JF-17 Block III represents a substantial improvement over Pakistan’s older JF-17 variants, Mirage III/V and F-7 aircraft continue to account for a sizeable portion of the PAF’s fighter inventory. The question is whether Pakistan Aeronautical Complex (PAC) and its Chinese partners can produce enough new aircraft quickly enough to replace the aging fleet.
The situation is more complicated than simply counting aircraft. Public fleet estimates vary considerably, and the precise number of operational aircraft available to the PAF at any given time is not publicly known. A recent assessment of South Asian air forces estimated that Pakistan operated around 21 fighter squadrons in 2025, with a fleet including approximately 75 F-16s, 20 J-10CEs, 156 JF-17s, 49 Mirage III, 37 Mirage V and 53 F-7PG aircraft. It also estimated only 23 JF-17 Block III aircraft in service at that point, with another 27 on order.
That makes the Block III transition particularly important.
The Block III is arguably the most sophisticated version of the JF-17. It introduces an AESA radar, improved avionics, enhanced electronic warfare capabilities and compatibility with modern beyond-visual-range weapons. Janes has reported that the PAF began inducting the Block III in 2023, while recent PAF imagery has shown the aircraft armed with China’s PL-15 long-range air-to-air missile and PL-10 imaging-infrared missile.
But the problem is scale.
A modern air force cannot replace several decades-old fighter fleets simply by introducing a few dozen new aircraft. Even if the JF-17 Block III is substantially more capable than the F-7PG or older Mirage variants, the PAF needs sufficient numbers to actually retire those aircraft while maintaining squadron strength.
This is where Pakistan’s fighter-modernisation challenge becomes visible.
FlightGlobal’s 2025 World Air Forces directory listed 123 active JF-17s with another 35 ordered, alongside 72 F-7s, 69 Mirage III variants and 90 Mirage V variants. These figures illustrate the scale of the replacement problem: Pakistan has a large number of legacy fighters to replace, but its modernisation pipeline is considerably smaller.
The age issue is particularly serious for the Mirage fleet. Pakistan has operated Mirage III and Mirage V aircraft since the 1960s, although individual airframes have undergone refurbishment and avionics upgrades. The country has maintained a domestic Mirage overhaul capability at PAC Kamra, which has helped extend the aircraft’s useful life.
That does not mean every Pakistani Mirage is unserviceable. Nor is it accurate to describe the entire F-7 fleet as “barely flight worthy” without access to PAF availability data. Aircraft age alone does not determine combat readiness; maintenance standards, remaining fatigue life, spare availability, inspection regimes and flying-hour restrictions are equally important.
Nevertheless, structural age and technological obsolescence eventually become increasingly difficult to overcome.
The F-7PG, for example, remains a fundamentally older-generation design. Scramble’s current order of battle still lists F-7PG aircraft with the PAF, including No. 20 Squadron as an operational conversion unit, while the newer JF-17 has progressively taken over the fighter’s role.
The PAF therefore faces a difficult transition: it has to retire old fighters while simultaneously increasing the production and induction rate of their replacements.
There is another complication—the JF-17 itself is not a single standard.
The PAF has accumulated Block I and Block II aircraft alongside Block III aircraft. Consequently, simply stating that Pakistan operates more than 150 JF-17s does not mean that it possesses 150 aircraft with the same radar, electronic-warfare capability or weapons integration.
The Block III represents a qualitative jump. Janes notes that the aircraft uses the KLJ-7A AESA radar, with improved multitargeting and resistance to jamming compared with the earlier radar fitted to Block II aircraft.
The PL-15 integration makes the difference even more significant. Recent PAF imagery showed a Block III carrying four PL-15 missiles, providing the aircraft with a considerably more modern BVR engagement capability than the earlier JF-17 configurations.
That creates an interesting force-structure problem for Pakistan.
The PAF may have a relatively large JF-17 fleet on paper, but its highest-end JF-17 capability remains concentrated in the Block III subset.
The Azerbaijan issue adds another dimension, although claims that Pakistan had to surrender six aircraft from its own small Block III inventory should be treated cautiously. Recent open-source analysis indicates that Azerbaijan has received at least nine Block III airframes and assesses that these were 2024-built aircraft rather than aircraft transferred from PAF stocks. The serial-number pattern supports that interpretation.
Therefore, the stronger story is not that Pakistan necessarily stripped its own operational squadrons to supply Azerbaijan. Rather, Pakistan’s industrial capacity is itself under pressure to satisfy domestic modernisation and export commitments simultaneously.
That is an important distinction.
Pakistan wants the JF-17 to become an export success, and Azerbaijan is a significant customer. The PAF simultaneously needs large numbers of newer aircraft to replace its ageing fleets. PAC therefore has to balance domestic requirements against export production.
The problem becomes particularly acute if Pakistan wants to retire Mirages and F-7s rapidly.
A fighter transition requires more than airframes. New pilots have to be trained, maintenance personnel converted, simulators acquired, weapons stocks built and infrastructure modified. A squadron cannot simply exchange eighteen old aircraft for eighteen Block IIIs overnight.
This may explain why the PAF’s transition is likely to be gradual rather than a sudden mass retirement.
There is also evidence that the PAF is already reorganising its fleet around this reality. Current open-source order-of-battle information places JF-17 Block III aircraft alongside older JF-17 variants, while F-7 aircraft continue to perform training and conversion roles.
For India, this has an important implication.
Pakistan’s fighter fleet should not be judged purely by its headline number of aircraft. The more meaningful metric is the number of modern, combat-capable fighters with AESA radar, modern electronic warfare, secure networking and long-range BVR weapons.
By that measure, the PAF’s transition is still underway.
The J-10CE provides another modern component, while the JF-17 Block III is progressively improving the quality of the larger JF-17 fleet. But replacing the Mirage and F-7 fleets at scale remains a substantial challenge.
Calling this a “downward spiral” may therefore be too strong based on publicly available evidence. The PAF is actively modernising, and its JF-17 Block III and J-10CE acquisitions represent genuine capability improvements.
The more defensible conclusion is that Pakistan faces a fighter-modernisation race against time.
Its legacy fleet is becoming increasingly difficult to sustain, while the number of genuinely modern replacements entering service remains limited relative to the size of the aircraft population that eventually needs to be replaced.

articles.title: 1987, 2019 and 2025: The Controversial History of Pakistan’s F-16 Losses and U.S. Assessments
articles.text:
The combat record of Pakistan’s F-16 fleet has repeatedly become entangled with something almost as important as the actual aircraft losses: the battle over the narrative surrounding those losses. From the mysterious circumstances surrounding an F-16 loss during the Soviet-Afghan War in 1987 to the fierce dispute following the 2019 India-Pakistan aerial engagement and renewed controversy after the 2025 conflict, Washington’s assessments have repeatedly attracted scrutiny in India.
It is important, however, to distinguish between what is documented and what remains an allegation. There is evidence that U.S. officials provided assessments that contradicted Indian claims, but there is not sufficient public evidence to conclusively establish that successive U.S. administrations deliberately participated in a coordinated cover-up of Pakistani F-16 losses.
The 1987 incident provides the earliest and perhaps most fascinating example.
On April 29, 1987, a PAF F-16A from No. 14 Squadron was lost during an interception mission near the Afghan border. Contemporary reporting from Afghanistan said an F-16 had been shot down by Afghan forces after entering Afghan territory and ignoring warnings. Pakistani officials initially confirmed that a Pakistani aircraft had been lost during aerial combat.
Later accounts, however, reconstructed a very different sequence of events. According to the detailed F-16 loss record, two Pakistani F-16As were attempting to intercept formations of Soviet/Afghan aircraft. During the engagement, the flight leader inadvertently locked onto his own wingman and fired an AIM-9-series missile, destroying the Pakistani aircraft. The aircraft-loss database records the incident on April 29, 1987.
This distinction matters enormously.
A PAF F-16 being shot down by an Afghan aircraft would represent a combat loss against an adversary. A PAF F-16 being destroyed by its own wingman would expose a very different problem involving identification, target discrimination and combat decision-making.
At the time, the F-16 was also a politically important symbol. Pakistan had only recently acquired the aircraft from the United States, and the platform was widely regarded as a major technological advantage for the PAF. A friendly-fire loss involving the aircraft would have been embarrassing for Pakistan and potentially uncomfortable for Washington.
But claiming that the U.S. government deliberately fabricated the Afghan-kill explanation requires evidence that is not currently available in the public record. The safer conclusion is that the public narrative surrounding the incident was inaccurate or incomplete and that the friendly-fire explanation emerged later.
The controversy returned dramatically in 2019.
Following the February 27, 2019 India-Pakistan aerial engagement, India claimed that an IAF MiG-21 Bison had shot down a Pakistani F-16 before the Indian aircraft itself was lost. Pakistan categorically denied losing an F-16.
Then came a remarkable U.S.-linked development.
Foreign Policy reported that two senior U.S. defence officials with direct knowledge of the matter said American personnel had physically counted Pakistan’s F-16s and found none missing. The report directly contradicted India’s claim.
The story quickly became an important piece of Pakistan’s information campaign. Pakistani state media highlighted the American assessment as evidence that India had fabricated the F-16 claim.
But there was an important complication.
The Pentagon subsequently said it was not aware of such an investigation, contradicting the impression created by the Foreign Policy report.
India, meanwhile, continued to maintain that a Pakistani F-16 had been destroyed. The IAF cited electronic signatures, imagery and other intelligence supporting its assessment.
Consequently, the 2019 episode should not simply be described as “America proved Pakistan did not lose an F-16.” The public record is considerably more complicated. An American publication cited unnamed U.S. officials claiming all Pakistani F-16s were accounted for, while the Pentagon said it was unaware of such an investigation.
That distinction is crucial.
The issue resurfaced again following Operation Sindoor in May 2025.
In August 2025, IAF Chief Air Chief Marshal A.P. Singh said India had destroyed at least five Pakistani fighter aircraft and one large aircraft during the operation.
By October, Singh provided additional details, saying that four to five Pakistani fighters, most likely F-16s, had been destroyed in long-range strikes, while additional fighter aircraft were hit on the ground.
Again, the claims remain contested and the exact aircraft-by-aircraft loss accounting is not publicly established to a standard that would eliminate every disagreement. Independent assessments have also urged caution. A later study of the 2025 conflict noted that radar disappearance alone cannot necessarily establish an aircraft kill and distinguished between claimed losses and visually documented losses.
Why does the F-16 generate such intense sensitivity in Pakistan?
The answer is partly technological and partly political. The F-16 has been one of Pakistan’s most important combat aircraft since the 1980s. Its reputation is tied closely to Pakistan’s perception of itself as possessing a credible counterweight to India’s larger fighter fleet.
Consequently, admitting an F-16 loss can have implications beyond the loss of one aircraft. It can affect perceptions of PAF competence, American technology, Pakistan’s air-combat capability and the credibility of its deterrence narrative.
Washington also has its own interests.
The United States has historically maintained a close defence relationship with Pakistan and has supplied F-16s under strict end-user arrangements. Those arrangements included requirements concerning accounting for the aircraft, making U.S. involvement in fleet inspections entirely plausible. Contemporary reporting in 2019 explicitly noted that Pakistan invited American personnel to count its F-16 fleet under the relevant end-user framework.
It does, however, explain why American assessments of Pakistani F-16 numbers carry disproportionate political weight.
The 2019 episode is particularly instructive because the American claim was immediately adopted by Pakistan as a rebuttal to India, even though the Pentagon subsequently distanced itself from the idea that it had conducted such an investigation.
The lesson for India is therefore not simply to dismiss every American assessment involving Pakistani aircraft. Rather, Indian intelligence and military assessments should be evaluated independently against multiple sources: satellite imagery, aircraft serial numbers, wreckage, electronic intelligence, radar tracks, communications intelligence and commercial imagery.

articles.title: Air Marshal Mishra: On 10 May, I cleared the S-400 to hit PAF AWACS at 314 km inside Pakistan
articles.text:
Air Marshal Jeetendra Mishra, who headed Western Air Command during Operation Sindoor, has given one of the most detailed first-person accounts yet of a long-range air defence engagement that Indian officials have described as among the farthest surface-to-air kills on record.
Speaking to Smita Prakash on the ANI Podcast, Mishra said he was in the command centre on 10 May when a Pakistan Air Force airborne early warning aircraft — an AWACS — was tracked trying to look into Indian airspace. The aircraft, he said, was linked to activity around PAF Base Mushaf at Sargodha. When it was still about 200 km from the border, he cleared an S-400 battery to fire. He confirmed the target was hit at a range of 314 km inside Pakistan.
That number has circulated in Indian briefings and later commentary since the operation. Then IAF chief Air Chief Marshal Amar Preet Singh had earlier said a large Pakistani aircraft — an AEW&C or ELINT platform — was engaged at about 300 km, calling it the longest surface-to-air kill the service could publicly discuss. Indian reports have often identified the aircraft as a Saab 2000 Erieye and placed the engagement near the Dinga area of Pakistani Punjab. Pakistan has not accepted that account.
Mishra’s value in the podcast is not a new slogan. It is the decision loop. An AWACS is not just another aircraft. It is a flying radar and command node: it sees fighters, missiles and drones far beyond a ground radar’s horizon and helps an air force manage the fight. Letting one sit off the border and “peek” is not a routine track. It is a choice about whether the other side is allowed to build a picture of Indian airspace. Mishra’s telling is that Western Air Command did not wait for the aircraft to come closer. The S-400 battery asked for clearance. He gave it. The shot went out at long range.
He also spoke about the wider contest around the S-400 itself. In the same conversation he claimed Pakistan tried, during and after the operation, to locate Indian S-400 batteries, including through spies and sleeper cells inside India. That is a serious allegation; it is his claim, not an independently published investigation in the open domain. What it does underline is how both sides treated the system as a centre of gravity. If a battery can reach hundreds of kilometres, the other air force has two problems at once: keep its AWACS alive, and find the launcher before the launcher finds the AWACS.

articles.text:

The aircraft had taken off from Pakistan Air Force Base Mushaf in Sargodha and was only 200 km from the border when he cleared an S-400 battery to engage it. He confirmed that the aircraft was hit 314 km inside Pakistan.
Air Marshal Jeetendra Mishra, speaking to the ANI Podcast, also said that air-to-ground missiles were used to strike some of the larger Pakistani radars, hinting that Harop loitering munitions carrying anti-radiation payloads were not the only systems used during the operation. However, it is not clear which anti-radiation missile was used in the conflict.
Since the IAF’s Rafale fleet does not currently operate an anti-radiation missile, it is possible that the missile was launched from a Sukhoi-30MKI, which can employ the Russian-origin Kh-31P and Kh-31PD supersonic anti-radiation missiles.
The operational range of the Russian-origin Kh-31P anti-radiation missile operated by India is approximately 110 kilometres. India also operates the upgraded Kh-31PD variant, reportedly acquired in 2019, which features an elongated fuselage and enhanced propulsion, extending its maximum range to approximately 250 kilometres. Both variants can fly at supersonic speeds of up to around Mach 3.5, allowing Indian Air Force Su-30MKI and MiG-29 aircraft to engage hostile air-defence radars from significant standoff distances.
During Operation Sindoor, the IAF reportedly destroyed two AN/TPS-43 radars located in Sukkur and Lahore, along with two AN/TPS-77 radars located at Arifwala and Chunian.
